In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of new methods of treatment of HIV/AIDS, the study of the molecular mechanisms of the action of antiviral drugs, as well as the search for new antiviral agents.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of LPV/r‐based ART in the real world is associated with lower virologic response rates compared to DRV/r‐based ART.
there is no evidence that any of the three boosted PI‐based regimens are superior to the others in terms of efficacy or tolerability.
there is no significant difference in long‐term effectiveness between LPV/r‐, DRV/r‐, and ATZ/r‐based ART regimens, and all of them can be used in clinical practice.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have found a significant association between the use of ART based on atazananavir-ritonavir (ATV/r), darunavir-ritonavir, and lopanivir-ritonavir and a lower risk of cardiovascular events.
the majority of people living with HIV (PLHIV) in Europe are on ART, and most of them are virally suppressed.

the long‐term effectiveness of the recommended ART based on boosted protease inhibitor (PI/r) regimens is high, with low rates of virological failure and drug discontinuation, and a high percentage of patients maintaining an undetectable viral load and a high CD4 count.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the long‐term efficacy of boosted protease inhibitor (PI/r)‐based ART in the ART‐experienced setting is similar to that in the naïve setting, and that the efficacy of these regimens is maintained in the long term.
